In Acts, believers (the apostles, Samaritans, Ephesian disciples) received the Spirit in a distinct experience after believing.
The purpose of Spirit baptism is power for witness (Acts 1:8), not salvation itself.
Classical Pentecostals hold that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6).
Wesleyan Holiness Pentecostals placed it after entire sanctification (three stages); Finished Work Pentecostals after conversion (two stages).

The narrative of Acts repeatedly separates faith and the reception of the Spirit.
It accounts for the transforming experience of hundreds of millions of Pentecostals and charismatics.
It expects New Testament power and gifts in the church today.
Reformed, Baptist and many evangelical scholars: 1 Corinthians 12:13 says all believers are baptised in the Spirit; Acts records unique transitional events.
Initial-evidence teaching lacks didactic support and can create two classes of Christians.
Historic churches locate the gift of the Spirit in baptism and chrismation/confirmation.
Pentecostals answer that Luke has a distinct theology of empowerment that complements Paul’s soteriological pneumatology (Roger Stronstad).
Many charismatics speak of "release" of the Spirit given in baptism, bridging the views.
Gave rise to the Pentecostal movement and charismatic renewal, now perhaps a quarter of world Christianity.
positions/spirit-baptism-at-conversion/o: Every Christian is baptised in the Holy Spirit at conversion-initiation; later experiences are renewed fillings or releases, not a second baptism.
positions/spirit-baptism-at-conversion/c: "By one Spirit are we all baptized into one body" (1 Cor 12:13) — Spirit baptism is universal among believers.
"If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his" (Rom 8:9).
The Acts episodes are transitional moments in salvation history (Jerusalem, Samaria, Gentiles, John’s disciples).
Believers are commanded to be filled continually (Eph 5:18), not to seek a second baptism.
positions/spirit-baptism-at-conversion/o: The historic Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant consensus that the Spirit is given in Christian initiation; articulated against Pentecostal subsequence by Frederick Dale Bruner (1970), James D. G. Dunn (Baptism in the Holy Spirit, 1970) and John Stott (Baptism and Fullness, 1964/1975).
positions/spirit-baptism-at-conversion/s: It rests on Paul’s explicit teaching rather than narrative precedent.
It affirms the full Christian standing of every believer.
Many continuationists hold it while affirming spiritual gifts today.
Pentecostals: it flattens Luke’s distinct theology of empowerment and the clear subsequence in Acts 8 and 19.
It can underplay the experiential dimension of the Spirit’s work.
Charismatic Catholics and Anglicans experience a definite "release" that seems more than ordinary growth.
positions/spirit-baptism-at-conversion/r: Proponents answer that they welcome subsequent fillings and experiences, but not as a second baptism.
Dunn and others grant that conversion-initiation in Acts was an experienced, often dramatic event.
positions/spirit-baptism-at-conversion/c: Framed evangelical responses to Pentecostal and charismatic renewal; many "Third Wave" charismatics adopted it (John Wimber).

Baptism is immersion of believers only.
Baptism is "for" (eis) the remission of sins, not a testimony to sins already forgiven.

It takes Acts 2:38 and Acts 22:16 in their most natural sense.
It unites believers’ baptism with the historic church’s conviction that baptism is for forgiveness.
It provides a clear, objective moment of assurance.
Baptists and evangelicals: it makes a rite necessary for salvation and comes close to works-righteousness.
It implies that sincere unimmersed believers are unforgiven — though Campbell himself (Lunenburg letter, 1837) refused to say so.
Paedobaptists: it rejects the baptism of most Christians.
Restorationists answer that baptism is God’s act, received by faith, and that Scripture itself joins the two.
The Lunenburg letter shows Campbell recognising Christians among the unimmersed, a stance many Disciples follow.
Distinctive of a family of churches with millions of members in North America, Africa and Asia.
Fuelled debates with Baptists in 19th-century America.
positions/quaker-inward-baptism/oneLine: The one baptism of the new covenant is the inward baptism of Christ with the Holy Spirit and fire; outward water baptism was a temporary Jewish-Christian rite and is not to be continued.
positions/quaker-inward-baptism/coreClai: John’s water baptism was preparatory; Christ baptises with the Spirit (Matt 3:11).
There is "one baptism" (Eph 4:5), which must be spiritual.
Outward rites can substitute for inward reality.
The Salvation Army likewise omits sacraments (from 1883), for different, pragmatic and theological reasons.
positions/quaker-inward-baptism/origin: George Fox and early Friends (1650s); systematised by Robert Barclay, An Apology for the True Christian Divinity (1676), Proposition 12.
positions/quaker-inward-baptism/stronges: It stresses inward reality over external form.
Paul says Christ did not send him to baptise but to preach (1 Cor 1:17).
It avoids divisive disputes over subjects and modes.
Almost all churches: Christ’s command (Matt 28:19) is permanent, and the apostles baptised with water after Pentecost (Acts 2:41; 10:47).
Rejecting the sacraments breaks continuity with the universal practice of the church.
Inward experience without outward signs can become individualistic.
positions/quaker-inward-baptism/response: Friends answer that the Great Commission speaks of baptising "into the name", i.e. into the power of God, not with water.
Salvationists stress that the sacraments are not forbidden but not necessary.
positions/quaker-inward-baptism/conseque: Distinctive mark of Quakers and the Salvation Army.
positions/docetism/oneLine: The divine Christ only seemed (dokein) to have a real body, to be born and to suffer; true divinity cannot be touched by flesh or pain.
positions/docetism/coreClaims/0: Matter and flesh are unworthy of, or incompatible with, the pure divine.
positions/docetism/coreClaims/1: Christ's body was a phantom or a heavenly, non-material body.
positions/docetism/coreClaims/2: The heavenly Christ did not truly suffer or die; in some versions he departed from the man Jesus before the cross, or another (Simon of Cyrene) was crucified in his place.
positions/docetism/coreClaims/3: Salvation is revelation of saving knowledge, not redemption of the body.
positions/docetism/origin: Opposed already in 1 John 4:2–3 and 2 John 7 and by Ignatius of Antioch (c. 110); held in varied forms by Cerinthus, Basilides, Valentinian Gnostics, Marcion and later Manichaeans.
positions/docetism/strongestArguments/0: It protects divine transcendence and impassibility, widely assumed in ancient philosophy.
positions/docetism/strongestArguments/1: It can appeal to Paul's ‘likeness’ language.
positions/docetism/strongestArguments/2: It made sense to ancient audiences familiar with gods appearing in human guise.
positions/docetism/strongestObjections/0: 1 John 4:2–3: ‘every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God.’
positions/docetism/strongestObjections/1: If Christ did not truly suffer, the cross, the Eucharist and Christian martyrdom are emptied of meaning (Ignatius).
positions/docetism/strongestObjections/2: The resurrection narratives stress a body of flesh and bones (Luke 24:39; John 20:27).
positions/docetism/strongestObjections/3: Salvation of the body requires that the Saviour truly took a body (Irenaeus, Tertullian, On the Flesh of Christ).
positions/docetism/responses/0: Docetists read the ‘flesh’ passages as accommodated appearances for weak believers.
positions/docetism/responses/1: Gnostic teachers argued that the spirit, not the body, is what is saved, so the Saviour need not have a material body.
positions/docetism/consequences/0: Its rejection made the reality of Christ's flesh, the bodily resurrection and the goodness of creation foundational to Christian orthodoxy.
positions/docetism/consequences/1: Shaped the earliest rule-of-faith formulas (‘born… suffered… crucified… buried’) in the Apostles' Creed.
positions/docetism/consequences/2: Echoes appear in later movements (Cathars, some Anabaptist ‘celestial flesh’ Christologies such as Melchior Hoffman's and Menno Simons').
positions/adoptionism/oneLine: Jesus was a righteous man whom God chose and adopted as his Son — at his baptism, resurrection or conception — rather than the eternal Son incarnate.
positions/adoptionism/coreClaims/0: Jesus was fully and only human (in early forms), born of Joseph and Mary or of the Virgin.
positions/adoptionism/coreClaims/1: God's Spirit or power came upon him (at baptism), making him Messiah and Son by adoption.
positions/adoptionism/coreClaims/2: His sonship was a reward for perfect obedience.
positions/adoptionism/coreClaims/3: (Spanish Adoptionism, 8th c., a different and more orthodox form) The eternal Son is Son by nature, but Christ in his humanity is Son by adoption.
positions/adoptionism/origin: Early Jewish-Christian Ebionites; Theodotus the Cobbler at Rome (c. 190) and Paul of Samosata (deposed 268). In 8th-century Spain, Elipandus of Toledo and Felix of Urgell taught that Christ's humanity was adopted; condemned at Frankfurt (794) under Charlemagne, after Alcuin's opposition.
positions/adoptionism/strongestArguments: The baptismal voice (‘Thou art my beloved Son’) echoes the royal adoption formula of Psalm 2:7.
Early preaching in Acts speaks of God making Jesus Lord and Christ at the resurrection.
It places Jesus' real human obedience at the centre.
positions/adoptionism/strongestObjection: It contradicts the pre-existence and agency in creation of the Son (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2).
A man adopted by grace differs only in degree from other saints; he could not unite God and humanity.
Against Spanish Adoptionism: sonship belongs to the person, not the nature; there is only one Son, so two sonships divide Christ (Alcuin).
positions/adoptionism/responses/0: Ebionites and Theodotians appealed to early synoptic and Acts traditions as more primitive than John.
positions/adoptionism/responses/1: Elipandus argued that he followed the Mozarabic liturgy's language of the ‘adopted man’ and was protecting Christ's full humanity.
positions/adoptionism/consequences/0: Shaped early creeds by provoking emphasis on the Son's eternal pre-existence.
positions/adoptionism/consequences/1: The Spanish controversy highlighted tensions between Mozarabic Christians under Muslim rule and the Frankish church.
positions/adoptionism/consequences/2: Modern historical-critical scholarship revived debate about ‘exaltation’ Christology in the earliest sources.
